L1@P0: Improving Backscatter Intensity Calibration
L2@P0: for Multispectral LiDAR
L3@P0: Shuo Shi, Shalei Song, Wei Gong, Lin Du, Bo Zhu, and Xin Huang, Senior Member, IEEE
L4@P0: Abstract—A wavelength-dependent light detection and ranging
L5@P0: (LiDAR) backscatter intensity calibration method was developed
L6@P0: to maximize the advantages of a multispectral LiDAR system. We
L7@P0: established a spectral ratio calibration method for multispectral
L8@P0: LiDAR and investigated the effective calibration procedure for the
L9@P0: mixed measurement of the effect of incident angle and surface
L10@P0: roughness. Experiment results showed that the proposed LiDAR
L11@P0: spectral ratio is insensitive to sensor-related factors and advantageous in calibrating the effect of incidence angle and surface
L12@P0: roughness. As the product of the LiDAR calibration procedure
L13@P0: based on spectral ratio, extended vegetation indexes significantly
L14@P0: improve the classification accuracy.
L15@P0: Index Terms—Calibration, light detection and ranging (LiDAR)
L16@P0: spectral ratio, multispectral LiDAR, remote sensing, vegetation
L17@P0: index.
L18@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L19@P0: LIGHT detection and ranging (LiDAR) has been widely
L20@P0: used to obtain surface geometry and to perform target
L21@P0: characterization. LiDAR echo measurement generates a point
L22@P0: cloud that represents the coordinates (x, y, z) of the object and
L23@P0: is frequently tagged with auxiliary variables. For each point,
L24@P0: the intensity (I) value is also simultaneously recorded. An improved automation of the classification and interpretation of
L25@P0: laser scanning data has thus become necessary. The use of
L26@P0: laser backscatter intensity data has led to improvements in
L27@P0: the development of automatic methods for tree species determination, canopy structure analysis [1], and fractional cover
L28@P0: measurement [2].
L29@P0: A wide range of LiDAR sensors that use multiple laser
L30@P0: wavelengths have been developed to further investigate the potential of laser backscatter intensity. Among these new LiDAR
L31@P0: sensors, the concept of multispectral (or hyperspectral) LiDAR
L32@P0: can produce one-shot topographic and multispectral intensity
L33@P0: information. A number of prototypes of multispectral LiDAR

L49@P0: systems, which are mainly laboratory based, have been developed [3]–[5]. The detection results of multispectral LiDAR
L50@P0: include point cloud and multispectral intensities: [x, y, z, I(λ)],
L51@P0: where I(λ) is the backscattered intensity, and I is a function of
L52@P0: laser wavelength λ. The selected laser wavelength λ leads to a
L53@P0: certain wavelength-dependent backscatter characteristic of the
L54@P0: sensed surface.
L55@P0: The great potential of multispectral LiDAR is based on the
L56@P0: differences in backscatter intensities at multiple wavelengths.
L57@P0: Backscatter intensity calibration is essential in studying the
L58@P0: characteristics of the sensed targets. Backscatter signals are
L59@P0: mainly affected by several factors, including instrumental and
L60@P0: atmospheric effects, target scattering characteristics, and measurement geometry [6]–[8]. Studies have focused on correction
L61@P0: techniques for adjusting the intensity variations of singlewavelengthLiDAR systemsandhave subsequentlydemonstrated
L62@P0: the availability of such correction methods [9]–[11]. However,
L63@P0: calibration procedures are usually complex and restricted to
L64@P0: some extent, and they contain complex parameters. Calibration
L65@P0: for multispectral LiDAR is particularly difficult, because of the
L66@P0: increase in the number of wavelengths. The same is particularly
L67@P0: true if a single-wavelength calibration method is employed.
L68@P0: In the present study, we maximize the advantages of multispectral LiDAR in terms of backscatter intensity calibration.
L69@P0: We develop a laboratory-based prototype of a multispectral
L70@P0: LiDAR [5] designed for vegetation applications. This system
L71@P0: is designed to take measurements at four wavelengths (556,
L72@P0: 670, 700, and 780 nm). Our study used data from this multispectral LiDAR. Specifically, we aim to achieve the following
L73@P0: objectives:
L74@P0: 1) to establish multispectral intensity calibration methods
L75@P0: based on the radar equation;
L76@P0: 2) to evaluate the capability for improvement of a calibration method for multispectral LiDAR;
L77@P0: 3) to study the effect of calibration on target classification,
L78@P0: given the necessity of conducting further investigations
L79@P0: on any possible intensity influencing factors of multispectral LiDAR detection.

L117@P1: B. Backscattering Characteristics of Multispectral LiDAR
L118@P1: Our study involves data from a multispectral LiDAR system
L119@P1: that is designed for vegetation applications [5]. The principle of
L120@P1: this multispectral LiDAR has been well established in the application of object identification and observation, particularly in
L121@P1: the monitoring of the growth and nutrition status of vegetation.
L122@P1: The operation of the multispectral LiDAR system is presented
L123@P1: as a block diagram in Fig. 1. Four laser wavelengths (556, 670,
L124@P1: 700, and 780 nm) are selected for the detection of leaf nitrogen
L125@P1: and chlorophyll content [12]. These four laser diodes are synthesized into a beam. An independent laser range sensor performs range measurements. The synthesized backscatter signals
L126@P1: are received by the Schmidt–Cassegrain telescope and divided
L127@P1: into four channels for photomultiplier detection. The backscatter intensities and range of the objects can then be obtained
L128@P1: through data acquisition and the processing of the subsystem
L129@P1: in a computer. All the transmitting and receiving facilities of
L130@P1: the LiDAR system are fixed on a motorized precision stage
L131@P1: to ensure scanning detection and synchronous signal reception. Through laser scanning and ranging, point cloud comprising probe points with geometric information (x, y, z) and
L132@P1: intensity (I) can be obtained.

L153@P1: III. METHOD
L154@P1: This study proposed a calibration method based on spectral
L155@P1: ratio with consideration of the advantage of multispectral signals. In addition, vegetation indexes that could help improve the
L156@P1: capability of object classification were established as products
L157@P1: of the calibration method.

L160@P1: combined into a beam to ensure that the near and far fields of
L161@P1: light overlap. This procedure causes the influences of the incidence angle and sensor factors within the footprint to become
L162@P1: similar at each laser wavelength. Thus, the calculation of spectral ratios should be insensitive to sensor-related factors and be
L163@P1: influenced primarily by the target characteristics.

L230@P2: B. Vegetation Index Extended by Spectral Ratio
L231@P2: By establishing a LiDAR calibration procedure based on
L232@P2: spectral ratio, multispectral LiDAR offers a unique advantage in
L233@P2: eliminating relevant parameters required in radar equation. This
L234@P2: advantage helps simplify the calibration procedure and improve
L235@P2: calibration accuracy. In addition to the calibration method,
L236@P2: LiDAR spectral ratios at multiwavelengths can be employed to
L237@P2: establish vegetation indexes.

L240@P2: remote sensing data [14]. Multispectral LiDAR is now considered as a new approach for measuring vegetation indexes [13],

L268@P2: IV. EXPERIMENT AND DISCUSSION
L269@P2: Laboratory measurements were performed to investigate the
L270@P2: effectiveness of the multispectral LiDAR calibration procedure
L271@P2: in the mixed backscatter intensity measurement of the incidence
L272@P2: angle effect, as well as the surface roughness of the target.
L273@P2: The calibration result was evaluated through a classification
L274@P2: experiment.
L275@P2: A. Calibration of Incidence Angle and Roughness Effects
L276@P2: Four kinds of objects, namely, healthy leaves of Platanus orientalis, deciduous leaves of P. orientalis, soil, and cement (see
L277@P2: Fig. 2), were selected to represent various degrees of surface
L278@P2: roughness. The instrument with four wavelengths was assumed
L279@P2: to be effective in discriminating the different objects. All operations were conducted in a darkroom to reduce the influence of
L280@P2: the environment factors. The multispectral laser light was horizontally transmitted toward the objects at a distance of 10 m.
L281@P2: The measurements of the four targets were taken with an incidence angle ranging from 0o to 80o to evaluate the influence
L282@P2: of the incidence angle.

L348@P4: V. CONCLUSION
L349@P4: This letter has presented a wavelength-dependent LiDAR
L350@P4: backscatter intensity calibration method that maximizes the
L351@P4: advantages of multispectral LiDAR. We established a spectral
L352@P4: ratio calibration method for multispectral LiDAR and investigated the effective calibration procedure for the mixed measurement of effects of incidence angle and surface roughness.
L353@P4: The LiDAR spectral ratio was insensitive to sensor factors and
L354@P4: advantageous in calibrating the effect of a known sensor inclination angle and the effect of a typically unknown target
L355@P4: inclination with respect to the sensor. Moreover, the vegetation
L356@P4: indexes produced by the LiDAR calibration procedure improved the classification accuracy.
L357@P4: Most calibration methods for LiDAR detection consider only
L358@P4: a single wavelength. The development of the spectral ratio
L359@P4: method improves the calibration procedure of multispectral
L360@P4: LiDAR. With the development of the multispectral LiDAR
L361@P4: system, the approach should be further tested, and additional
L362@P4: calibration factors should be considered. Therefore, this study
L363@P4: can be regarded as a practical solution to the calibration problem of multispectral LiDAR.
